A.explanation: This is half the correct value and results from using $n = 4$ or dividing by an extra factor of 2 in $d \sin\theta = n\lambda$.

B.explanation: With $d = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$, $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ and $n = 2$, $\lambda = d\sin\theta / n = 5.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

C.explanation: This is twice the correct value and results from using first order $n = 1$ instead of second order $n = 2$.

D.explanation: This is 100 times too large and results from using $d = 1/5000 \text{ cm}$ without converting cm to m.

hints: Notice the grating is given as 5000 lines per cm, so first convert this to the slit separation $d$ in metres.
Recall the normal-incidence grating equation $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ with order $n = 2$ and $\theta = 30^{\circ}$.
Calculate $d = 1/N$ where $N = 500000 \text{ m}^{-1}$, then use $\lambda = d\sin30^{\circ}/2$ and check the power of ten.
walkthrough: Find the grating spacing $d$ from lines per unit length. $N = 5000 \text{ per cm} = 500000 \text{ per m}$, so $d = 1/N = 1/500000 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$.
State the governing rule for normal incidence: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $n$ is the order of maximum.
Identify the values for this second-order maximum: $n = 2$ and $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, so $\sin\theta = 0.5$.
Rearrange and substitute with units: $\lambda = d\sin\theta / n = (2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m})(0.5)/2$.
Evaluate to $\lambda = 0.50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, which is visible light. This is option B.
